# Gronify

> Local-first, standalone CLI for turning JSON into greppable paths, searching those paths, and round-tripping gron output back to JSON.

Gronify is a TypeScript CLI that flattens JSON documents into one gron-style assignment per path, searches those paths with plain text or extended regex, and unflattens gron output back into valid JSON. Flattening, unflattening, and search are all built in — no external command-line tools such as grep or fastgron are required at runtime.

The CLI reads from files or stdin and writes to stdout, so it composes naturally with pipes, redirection, and other shell tools. Optional flags control colored output, pretty indentation, output files, case-sensitive and inverted matching, match counts, result caps, key sorting, and exit codes.

Gronify is designed for platform engineers, SREs, developer-experience teams, support engineers, and developers who inspect large JSON payloads in CI logs, service responses, support bundles, generated configuration, or incident debugging sessions.

The project is open source under the MIT license. The current release is 1.2.0 (2026-10-31).

## Features

- Flatten JSON files or stdin into gron-style path assignments, streaming multi-gigabyte inputs in about 100 MB of memory.
- Unflatten gron files or stdin back into JSON, also streaming.
- Search flattened paths with plain text, extended regex, case-sensitive matching, inverted matching, and match counts.
- Cap the output with `search -m/--max-count` and `flatten --limit`. Gronify stops reading the input at the cap, so a large file returns in milliseconds when the cap is hit early. (1.2.0)
- Sort object keys at every level with `--sort` for stable, diffable output. The default is document order. (1.2.0)
- Opt in to grep-style exit codes with `search --exit-status`. (1.2.0)
- Keep numbers exactly as written: `12345678901234567890` and `1.10` come out unchanged.
- Write output files atomically with `-o`: the target is replaced only after the run succeeds.
- Use stdin/stdout workflows so Gronify can sit inside shell pipelines.
- Format terminal output with optional colors and pretty indentation.

## Requirements

- Node.js 20 or newer.
- npm 10 or newer (only when building from source).
- No external binaries are required at runtime.
- Gronify 1.2.0 or newer for `-m/--max-count`, `--limit`, `--sort`, and `--exit-status`. Version 1.1.0 stops with `error: unknown option '-m'`. Check with `gronify --version` or `gronify search --help | grep -e --max-count`.

## Installation

### npm

```bash
npm install -g gronify
# or run it once without installing
npx gronify --help
```

Update an existing install with `npm install -g gronify@latest`.

### Homebrew

Homebrew installs Gronify together with its dependencies:

```bash
brew install 1solomonwakhungu/tap/gronify
```

The formula is maintained in the [Homebrew tap](https://github.com/1solomonwakhungu/homebrew-tap).

### Release Archive

Download the archive for the latest version from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/1solomonwakhungu/gronify/releases). The executable requires Node.js 20 or newer.

### Build from Source

1. Clone and build Gronify.

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/1solomonwakhungu/gronify.git
   cd gronify/src/packages/cli
   npm ci
   npm run build
   ```

2. Link the local CLI.

   ```bash
   npm link
   gronify --help
   ```

## Command Reference

### Global Options

| Option                | Description                                                                   |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--color`             | Enable colored output when the terminal supports it.                          |
| `--no-color`          | Disable colored output.                                                       |
| `--pretty`            | Add indentation/grouping to formatted output.                                 |
| `-o, --output <file>` | Write output to a file instead of stdout. The file is replaced atomically.    |
| `-h, --help`          | Show help.                                                                    |
| `-V, --version`       | Show the CLI version.                                                         |

### `flatten [file]`

Converts JSON to gron format. If `file` is omitted, Gronify reads from stdin. Keys come out in document order unless `--sort` is given.

**Signature:** `gronify flatten [file]`

#### Flatten Options

| Option        | Description                                                                                  |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--limit <n>` | Stop after `n` lines of output and stop reading the input. `n` must be a positive integer.   |
| `--sort`      | Sort object keys at every level by UTF-16 code unit. Array order is unchanged.               |

**Examples:**

```bash
gronify flatten data.json
cat data.json | gronify flatten
gronify flatten --sort --limit 100 data.json
```

### `unflatten [file]`

Converts gron format back to JSON. If `file` is omitted, Gronify reads from stdin.

**Signature:** `gronify unflatten [file]`

**Examples:**

```bash
gronify unflatten data.gron
cat data.gron | gronify unflatten
gronify --output data.json unflatten data.gron
```

`unflatten` streams. Gron in document order (each container before its children, siblings together, array indexes ascending), which is what `flatten` and `flatten --sort` write, converts in one pass at any size. Out-of-order input is rebuilt in memory only while the first 16 MiB are read; after that it fails with `line N: ...`. Do not run plain `sort` on gron you plan to unflatten: it puts `[10]` before `[2]`.

### `search <file_or_term> [term]`

Searches flattened JSON paths. Pass both a file and term, or pipe JSON to stdin and pass only the search term.

**Signature:** `gronify search <file_or_term> [term]`

#### Search Options

| Option                 | Description                                                                                          |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-r, --regex`          | Use extended regular expressions.                                                                    |
| `-c, --case-sensitive` | Match case sensitively.                                                                              |
| `--count`              | Print only the match count.                                                                          |
| `-v, --invert-match`   | Show lines that do not match.                                                                        |
| `-m, --max-count <n>`  | Stop after `n` matching lines (`n` non-matching lines with `-v`) and stop reading the input.         |
| `--sort`               | Sort object keys at every level, as for `flatten`. Ignored with `--count`.                           |
| `--exit-status`        | Exit 1 when nothing matches, like `grep`. Errors then exit 2 instead of 1.                           |

Plain search terms are case-insensitive substring matches.

**Examples:**

```bash
gronify search data.json "user"
gronify search data.json --regex "user\.[a-z]+"
cat data.json | gronify search "name"
gronify search data.json --count "field"
gronify search data.json --case-sensitive "Service"
gronify search data.json -m 20 "error"
gronify search --exit-status config.json -m 1 "debug = true"
```

### Result Caps

`search -m/--max-count <n>` and `flatten --limit <n>` stop after `n` lines, following `grep -m`. Gronify stops reading the input at the cap, so the rest of the file is never read or validated; a 5 GB file whose first match is near the start returns in milliseconds, and `cat huge.json | gronify search -m 5 term` ends instead of waiting. The exit status is 0. When a cap ended the run, one line goes to stderr and stdout holds only gron lines:

```text
Stopped after 20 matches (--max-count); there may be more
```

With `--count`, `-m` counts up to `n`. With `-o`, the capped output is committed atomically. With `--sort`, the cap applies to the sorted order, so a document whose root is an object is read to the end first.

### Sorting Keys

The default is document order. `--sort` on `flatten` or `search` sorts the keys of every object at every level:

```bash
echo '{"b":1,"a":{"d":4,"c":3},"10":0,"2":0}' | gronify flatten --sort
```

```text
json = {}
json["10"] = 0
json["2"] = 0
json.a = {}
json.a.c = 3
json.a.d = 4
json.b = 1
```

- Keys are compared by UTF-16 code unit, like JavaScript's default `sort()`, so `"10"` comes before `"2"`.
- Each key's subtree stays together, and array elements keep their index order (`[2]` before `[10]`).
- The output is stable: two documents that differ only in key order give identical lines, so `diff <(gronify flatten --sort a.json) <(gronify flatten --sort b.json)` shows real changes.
- The output is in document order, so `gronify flatten --sort data.json | gronify unflatten` streams in one pass.
- This is not gron's order. gron puts bare keys (`json.b`) before bracketed keys (`json["10"]`) at each level and compares UTF-8 bytes, so the two outputs can differ. It is also not what plain `sort` on the lines gives.
- A top-level array is sorted record by record as it streams. An object is held until it closes, using up to 64 MiB of memory and then a temp file in `$TMPDIR`. Set `GRONIFY_SORT_MEMORY` (bytes, or a size such as `256MiB`) to change the 64 MiB.

### Exit Codes

| Code | Meaning                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `0`  | Success, including a `search` with no matches (the default), a run stopped by `-m`/`--limit`, and a closed output pipe such as `\| head`.                     |
| `1`  | Failure: invalid JSON or gron, an unreadable or missing file, no input, an invalid option value, or an unknown option. With `search --exit-status`: no match. |
| `2`  | Only with `search --exit-status`: any failure from the list above.                                                                                          |

### Streaming and Large Inputs

`flatten`, `search`, and `unflatten` read their input in chunks and write output as they go. Peak memory stays around 100 MB whether the input is 20 MB or several gigabytes. Measured on an Apple M5 Pro with Node 22:

| Input                    | Command          | Time   | Peak RSS |
| ------------------------ | ---------------- | ------ | -------- |
| 3.50 GB JSON             | `flatten`        | 22.1 s | 98 MB    |
| 3.50 GB JSON             | `search --count` | 24.5 s | 96 MB    |
| 3 GB gron                | `unflatten`      | 7.3 s  | 100 MB   |
| 1.2 GiB array of records | `search -m 5`    | 0.03 s | 57 MB    |

- Input is strict JSON. Errors report the byte offset, line, and column.
- Numbers are printed exactly as written: `12345678901234567890`, `1.10`, `1e2`, and `-0` come out unchanged through `flatten`, `search`, and `unflatten`.
- Output starts before the input has been read in full, so when input turns out to be invalid, stdout may already hold some lines. The error message and non-zero exit code are always produced; check the exit status or use `set -o pipefail`.
- With `-o`, output goes to a temporary file that replaces the target only after the run succeeds. A failed run leaves an existing target untouched, and `-o` may name the input file.
- Colored `unflatten` output is built in memory; use `--no-color` for very large inputs.

## Usage Examples

### Flatten a JSON File

```bash
gronify flatten data.json
```

### Flatten JSON from stdin

```bash
echo '{"service":"api","retries":2}' | gronify flatten
```

### Unflatten gron Output Back to JSON

```bash
gronify flatten data.json | gronify unflatten
```

### Search Flattened Paths

```bash
gronify search data.json "service"
gronify search data.json --regex "users\[[0-9]+\]\.name"
gronify search data.json --case-sensitive "Service"
gronify search data.json --count "error"
```

### Use Gronify in a Pipeline

```bash
curl -s https://example.com/payload.json | gronify search --regex "metadata|status"
```

## Demo

### Sample Payload

Create a sample payload:

```bash
cat > demo.json <<'JSON'
{
  "service": {
    "name": "checkout",
    "status": "degraded"
  },
  "deployments": [
    { "region": "us-central1", "version": "2026.05.22" },
    { "region": "us-east1", "version": "2026.05.21" }
  ]
}
JSON
```

### Flatten the Payload

```bash
gronify flatten demo.json
```

Output:

```text
json = {}
json.service = {}
json.service.name = "checkout"
json.service.status = "degraded"
json.deployments = []
json.deployments[0] = {}
json.deployments[0].region = "us-central1"
json.deployments[0].version = "2026.05.22"
json.deployments[1] = {}
json.deployments[1].region = "us-east1"
json.deployments[1].version = "2026.05.21"
```

### Search for Operationally Relevant Fields

```bash
gronify search demo.json --regex "status|version"
```

Output:

```text
json.service.status = "degraded"
json.deployments[0].version = "2026.05.22"
json.deployments[1].version = "2026.05.21"
```

### Round-Trip Back to JSON

```bash
gronify flatten demo.json | gronify unflatten
```

Output:

```json
{"service":{"name":"checkout","status":"degraded"},"deployments":[{"region":"us-central1","version":"2026.05.22"},{"region":"us-east1","version":"2026.05.21"}]}
```

Add `--pretty` (`gronify flatten demo.json | gronify --pretty unflatten`) for indented output, which matches `JSON.stringify(value, null, 2)`.

### Stop After the First Match

```bash
gronify search demo.json -m 1 "version"
```

Output (the second line is on stderr):

```text
json.deployments[0].version = "2026.05.22"
Stopped after 1 match (--max-count); there may be more
```

## Pipeline Compositions

### Inspect a Remote API Response

```bash
curl -s https://example.com/payload.json | gronify flatten
```

### Search a Remote Payload

```bash
curl -s https://example.com/payload.json | gronify search --regex "metadata|status"
```

### Filter and Reconstruct

Flatten, search for specific paths, and unflatten the matching subset back into JSON:

```bash
gronify search data.json "deployments" | gronify unflatten
```

### Count Matches

```bash
gronify search data.json --count "error"
```

### Case-Sensitive Search

```bash
gronify search data.json --case-sensitive "Service"
```

### Look at a Large File Without Printing All of It

```bash
gronify search huge.json --count "error"   # how many matches, before printing any
gronify search huge.json -m 20 "error"     # the first 20 matches, then stop reading
gronify flatten --limit 50 huge.json       # the first 50 lines
```

### Use the Exit Status in a Script

```bash
if gronify search --exit-status config.json -m 1 "debug = true" > /dev/null 2>&1; then echo "debug is on"; fi
```

### Chain with Standard Shell Tools

```bash
gronify flatten --sort data.json
gronify flatten data.json | wc -l
gronify search data.json "user" | head -20
```

## Use Cases

### Incident Response

Find status, version, region, and error fields in service payloads without opening an editor.

```bash
gronify search payload.json --regex "status|version|error"
```

### CI Investigation

Inspect generated manifests and artifacts with grep-compatible output that fits existing scripts.

```bash
gronify flatten build-output.json | grep "artifact"
```

### Support Bundles

Search deeply nested exports locally while keeping customer data inside your shell workflow.

```bash
gronify search support-bundle.json "customer"
```

### Configuration Review

Compare meaningful paths instead of visually tracing braces through a large document. `--sort` gives both versions the same key order, so `diff` shows only real changes.

```bash
diff <(gronify --no-color flatten --sort old.json) <(gronify --no-color flatten --sort new.json)
```

## Troubleshooting

### `npm test` Fails Before Running Assertions

Build first so `dist/index.js` exists:

```bash
npm run build
npm test
```

### JSON Does Not Flatten

Validate that the input is valid JSON and that files passed to `flatten` are readable from the current shell.

### No Output from Search

Verify the search term matches the flattened path format. Use `gronify flatten --limit 50 <file>` first to see the paths, then refine the search term.

### `error: unknown option '-m'`

The installed Gronify is older than 1.2.0. Update with `npm install -g gronify@latest` or `brew upgrade gronify`, or cap the output with `| head -n 20` instead.

## Architecture

Gronify is a standalone TypeScript CLI built with commander.js for the command interface and chalk for colored terminal output. The CLI processes JSON locally — no data is sent to any external service.

The source code is organized under `src/packages/cli` within the repository. Integration tests run the built CLI directly and require no external binaries.

## Repository Layout

```text
.
|-- branding/              # Logo and icon assets
|-- landing-page/          # Next.js marketing/demo page
|-- scripts/               # Repository validation and package discovery helpers
|-- src/
|   |-- README.md          # Source tree orientation
|   `-- packages/cli/      # TypeScript CLI package
`-- .github/               # CI, Dependabot, and contribution templates
```

## Development

The CLI package lives in `src/packages/cli`.

```bash
cd src/packages/cli
npm ci
npm run build
npm test
```

Useful package scripts:

```bash
npm run lint
npm run format:check
npm run build
npm test
npm run audit
```

## FAQ

**Does Gronify require fastgron or grep?**
No. Flattening, unflattening, and search are all built into the standalone CLI.

**Can I use Gronify on Windows?**
Yes. Install from npm, use the release archive for your platform or Homebrew where supported, or build the TypeScript CLI from source with Node.js 20 or newer.

**How large a file can Gronify handle?**
`flatten`, `search`, and `unflatten` stream, so peak memory stays around 100 MB whether the input is 20 MB or several gigabytes. With `-m` or `--limit`, Gronify stops reading once the cap is reached.

**Does `--sort` produce the same order as gron?**
No. `--sort` compares keys by UTF-16 code unit at each level, keeps each subtree together, and leaves array order alone. gron puts bare keys before bracketed ones and compares UTF-8 bytes.

**Why do the integration tests fail before assertions run?**
Run `npm run build` first, so that `dist/index.js` exists before the integration tests start.

**Does Gronify send JSON to a service?**
No. Gronify is local-first. Every payload is processed by the CLI on your own machine.
